Fit vs. Fat: The rise of extreme food

Writer, DJ and chef Andrew Levins says he hasn't seen much overlap between the "gym-selfie squad" and "deep-fried Cornetto brigade", but suggests the popularity of extreme junk food on social media is a retaliation against the green-juice guzzling fitness crew.

"Some people post a video of them doing 400 squats and getting a new PB [personal best]," he says.

"It gains them 100 likes and a handful of comments like 'Damn!', 'Lookin' good!', and 'Would!' that makes them feel better about themselves.

"A less healthy friend will see that video and think, 'I want 100 likes and a handful of comments but I hate exercise. What's the complete opposite of 400 squats?'. The answer to that question is a quadruple beef burger with doughnuts for buns and covered in a different kind of PB: peanut butter."

(Op Ed) Google Can't Ignore The Android Update Problem Any Longer

It helps the cellular providers to lock down all updates to their low-end Android phones because users have to buy a replacement phone every 18 to 24 months to stay current with the O/S and features. Plus, it eliminates the risk of bricking the phone with an update. If the phones become compromised by new hacks, oh well, the consumer will just have to pay for a new phone. Cell providers have every incentive to drag their feet on this. How Google could realign the incentives of the cellular providers is the big question.

I don't think they're ignoring it as such, Google have made a massive effort to move a lot of their new features into support libraries that are compatible on the most commonly used platforms. Rather than baking fancy widgets into specific versions of Android, the developer has to include the right widget into their app, and update it whenever a new version is available.

This doesn't allow any of the updates like Doze mode to be backported of course, but it makes life far better for app users and developers. Hopefully Google will work with OEMs better in future to improve update speeds, but with my Samsung running 4.1.2, I'm not holding my breath.

I finished C25K on Friday. I ran 30 minutes, covering ~6.25 km. So for my next goal I want to get up to ~10 km. But the B210k plan I found has me going back to walking intervals, and frankly I'm past that stage. I'm thinking of just increasing my running time by 10% a week until I hit my target, but if anyone has a better idea, I'm all ears.

Congrats on finishing! Your plan sounds good to me, although I would recommend turning one of your runs into a long run, and keeping the others around 5k. When I finished C25K, I added an extra day of running and increased that day slowly. I found that to work really well.

Best of luck my friend.

To get me past the 5K point, I started adding interval sprints to my work out. Once every two weeks or so, I would run a session of:

  • Run as hard as I could for a lap
  • Walk or jog really slowly until I felt like I could sprint another lap
  • Repeat 3 more times

It really made a difference for me on my long runs where I was able to run longer without getting as tired. I'm sure there's a lot of scientific and fitness who-ha about why it works, but it just felt like my cardio-vascular fitness was reaching a new/higher "normal" after a while. And the results seemed to be really obvious to me very quickly. I'm not up to sprinting for 1/2 a mile with a 1/2 mile cooldown. And I'm gearing up for my first half marathon in Sept and things are looking good for it.

Looks like I am a bit late to the party. I agree with the other two comments but would like to add one thing. You should pick a new goal. Previously your goal was "Finish C25k". Your new goal might be "Run 10 miles", "run a 7 minute mile", "Break a 20 minute 5k" or "Race a half marathon". It doesn't really matter what it is. Those were just some suggestions, yours might be something different. My point is, you should let your goal determine your next steps.
